short: The first British heavy tank that one man could drive by himself.
full:
Earlier heavy tanks took four men to steer: a driver, a brakesman and two gearsmen working the secondary gears to hand signals in a compartment too loud for speech. The Mark V replaced all that with Walter Wilson's epicyclic steering gear and a purpose-built 150 hp Ricardo engine, so a single driver controlled the machine and the rest of the crew could fight it. A raised rear cab, better vision and a stronger unditching gear completed the design. Metropolitan Carriage of Birmingham built 400, half male and half female.

Sixty supported the Australian Corps at Hamel on 4 July 1918, a set-piece of artillery, infantry, tanks and air supply that took its objectives in ninety-three minutes and was studied as a model for the rest of the war. Mark Vs led at Amiens on 8 August and through the Hundred Days. Britain later shipped them to White Russian forces; the Red Army captured many and kept them into the 1920s, and four served Estonia until 1940. British service ended as faster medium tanks came in.
